subject: data-analytics
question: What was September's monthly churn rate, in percent (share of starting subscribers who cancelled)?

failure.misconception: Using the ending count as the denominator
failure.explanation: Churn as defined here is the share of subscribers at the start of the period who cancelled: 60 / 1,000 = 6%. The ending count of 1,200 includes 260 new sign-ups who could barely have churned yet, which understates churn - and the error grows with faster acquisition.
failure.why_convincing: 1,200 is 'the subscriber base' at the time of reporting.

valid_evidence.summary: The 1,200 includes 260 subscribers who joined during September.

counterexamples: Signing up many new customers would lower this 'churn' even if cancellations rose.

hints.text: Check which subscribers could have cancelled during the month.
Step 2 picks the ending subscriber count.
Churn is measured against the base at the start of the period.
Divide cancellations by starting subscribers.
Step 2 is wrong: the base is the 1,000 starting subscribers, so churn is 6%.

debrief: Rates need the right denominator: the population at risk. Using the end-of-period count lets growth hide churn.

subject: data-analytics
question: What did it cost, in rupees, to acquire each customer through ads?
ai_claim: 600. Rs 6,00,000 of ad spend over 1,000 new customers is Rs 600 per customer.

ai_solution.text: So acquiring a customer through ads cost Rs 600.

failure.misconception: Dividing ad spend by customers who did not come from ads
failure.explanation: 400 of the 1,000 customers arrived organically or by referral, at no ad cost. Paid CAC divides ad spend by customers acquired through ads: 6,00,000 / 600 = Rs 1,000. The blended figure (Rs 600) makes ads look 40% cheaper than they are.
failure.why_convincing: Blended CAC is a real metric, and the division is correct.

valid_evidence.summary: 400 customers came from organic and referral channels.

counterexamples: More organic sign-ups would make the ads look cheaper without any change in ad performance.

hints.text: Check which customers the ad spend actually acquired.
Step 2 uses all new customers.
Paid CAC divides paid spend by paid customers only.
Divide the spend by the 600 ad customers.
Step 2 is wrong: only 600 customers came from ads, so paid CAC is Rs 1,000.

debrief: Match numerator and denominator: paid spend with paid customers. Blended metrics are useful for overall efficiency, but they misstate the cost of any single channel.

subject: data-analytics
question: What is the Net Promoter Score?

table.title: Survey: 'How likely are you to recommend us?' (0-10), 100 responses

ai_claim: 60. Promoters are those who scored 7 to 10 (80%), detractors scored 0 to 6 (20%), so NPS = 80 - 20 = 60.

failure.explanation: In NPS, promoters score 9 or 10; scores of 7 and 8 are passives, who count in the total but in neither group. Promoters are 50%, detractors 20%, so NPS = 50 - 20 = 30.

counterexamples: Moving every 7-8 response to 9 would change the NPS, which shows passives are not promoters.

hints.text: Recall the score bands NPS uses.
Step 1 counts 7s and 8s as promoters.
Promoters are 9-10 only; 7-8 are passives.
Recompute with promoters = 50.
Step 1 is wrong: 7-8 are passives. NPS is 50 - 20 = 30.

debrief: Named metrics have fixed definitions. Using a variant silently makes numbers incomparable with benchmarks and with past reports.

subject: data-analytics
question: Does the 40% rise in page views per session show that the redesign improved engagement?

before_after.title: Website redesign, 4 weeks before vs after

ai_claim: Yes. Visitors now view 40% more pages per session, which means they are more engaged with the site.

ai_solution.text: Page views per session rose from 4.0 to 5.6.
More page views means more time spent exploring content.
Exploring more content means greater engagement.

failure.misconception: Treating a vanity metric as evidence of value
failure.explanation: More page views can mean people are lost. Conversion fell from 3.1% to 2.4%, and 'can't find' tickets more than doubled: users click through more pages because they cannot find what they want. Evaluate the redesign by outcome metrics (conversion, task success), with page views as a diagnostic at most.
failure.why_convincing: Page views are easy to count and usually move with interest.

canonical_solution: No: falling conversion and rising 'can't find' tickets suggest the extra page views reflect confusion, not engagement.

valid_evidence.summary: Conversion fell from 3.1% to 2.4%; 'can't find' tickets rose from 120 to 310 per week.
Users hunting for a missing checkout link also generate extra page views.

hints.text: Look at the other two metrics.
Step 2 assumes more page views means more interest.
Activity metrics can rise for bad reasons; outcome metrics show value.
Compare conversion and support tickets before and after.
Step 2 is wrong: the other metrics suggest users are lost. Judge by conversion and task success.

repair: Evaluate with outcome metrics (conversion, task completion), and treat page views as a diagnostic.
debrief: Vanity metrics go up for good and bad reasons alike. Pair every activity metric with an outcome metric before calling a change a success.
